plan.title: What to plant, month by month
plan.sub: Each month lists the crops with enough rain and not too much heat.
plan.none: Too dry or too hot for the crops we know.
plan.note: A crop is listed for a month when the rain across its season covers at least three quarters of what it needs, and the heat stays under its limit.
place.gateSub: Every page uses the same field, so you only enter it once.
footer.note: Guidance only. Check with your extension officer before you sow.
plan.horizonNote: The months repeat each year because this is a typical year, not a forecast. Use the years ahead to plan seed, land and labour.
horizon.label: How far ahead do you want to plan?
horizon.note: We have recent averages, not a year-by-year forecast. Each year uses the same typical pattern — plan your rhythm, then check the season as it comes.
setup.title: Your field, your priorities
setup.sub: Tell us a little more and we will change the advice.
setup.note: This changes the order of the crops, not the weather.
rotation.title: Plan a rotation
rotation.sub: A rotation is the order you plant crops across seasons. Change the crops and watch what happens to the soil.
rotation.compareSub: Both plans use the same weather, soil and priorities. Only the order of crops changes.
rotation.need: Needs about {mm} mm of water and {days} days each season.
rotation.note.short: Add another season to see how a rotation builds up.
rotation.note.legumeFirst: A legume before a cereal feeds the next crop — it leaves nitrogen in the ground.
rotation.note.legume: {crop} is a legume. It puts nitrogen back into the soil.
rotation.note.noLegume: No legume here, so the soil gives more than it gets back.
rotation.note.repeat: Two crops from the same family in a row take out the same nutrients.
rotation.note.variety: Mixing crop families and root depths keeps the soil in better shape.
rotation.note.soil: Some of these crops do not suit {soil} soil.
rotation.note.cover: A long-season crop keeps the ground covered into the dry months.
rotation.why.title: Why rotations protect the soil
rotation.why.1: Different crops take different nutrients. Planting the same family again and again empties the soil.
rotation.why.2: Groundnut and cowpea are legumes. They work with bacteria on their roots to put nitrogen back.
rotation.why.3: Deep roots (millet, sorghum, cassava) break up hard ground; shallow roots use the top layer.
rotation.why.4: Keeping the ground covered through the dry months slows erosion and holds water in the soil.
rotation.disclaimer: A simple guide built from crop families, the soil you described and local rain — not a soil test. Ask your extension officer before changing a rotation.
rotation.ctaSub: See how the order of your crops protects the soil over several seasons.
rotation.note.builds: Across the whole plan, more nitrogen goes back into the soil than comes out.
weather.shift: These are recent averages, not a forecast. Rain and heat shift from year to year, so check the season ahead before you sow.
catalogue.title: Crops and fruits grown here
catalogue.sub: Real photographs, so you can recognise each one. We only rank a crop when we have measured water and heat needs for it.
catalogue.annualSub: Planted and harvested within one season. These are the crops the monthly plan talks about.
catalogue.orchardSub: These take years to establish, so they are not part of a monthly sowing plan or a rotation.
catalogue.notRanked: Not enough data to rank yet
catalogue.note: Photographs and licence details are listed in CREDITS.md. Scientific names come from the shared crop catalogue; local-language names are being added with native speakers.
